{"id": "70:10/q03", "question": "What does ḥamīm mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether closeness here is restricted to kinship or also includes intimate friendship and alliance.", "positions": [{"id": "70:10/q03/p1", "position": "A close blood relative or kinsperson.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, cited by al-Wāḥidī, adds mutual protective anger. Al-Ṭabrisī derives the sense from nearness and cites poetry. Ibn al-Jawzī notes the related senses hot water and ḥamiyya, hot anger or jealousy, while also listing close relative. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ adds one whose affairs a person cares about."}, {"id": "70:10/q03/p2", "position": "An intimate, close friend or ally, whether related by blood or not.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash, reported by al-Ṭabrisī, defines one specially loved regardless of blood tie and explains al-ḥāmah as one's close circle. Abū ʿUbayda and al-Dāmghānī allow both relative and intimate; Ibn ʿAṭiyya includes an ally. Ibn al-Jawzī's other lexical senses, hot water and hot anger or jealousy, are not proposed as this verse's referent."}]}
{"id": "70:10/q04", "question": "What does the verse say close people fail to ask on that Day?", "turns_on": "Whether 'ask' concerns another's condition, a request for assistance, sins or intercession, accountability, or summons; the active and passive readings support different construals, and seeing in 70:11 can explain recognition or why inquiry is unnecessary.", "positions": [{"id": "70:10/q04/p1", "position": "They do not ask after one another's condition, or even speak, because terror leaves each absorbed in his own plight.", "reasons": "Muqātil adds that the man does not speak to kin. Al-Farrāʾ says they recognize one another briefly, then recognition ends. Al-Wāḥidī compares the mother forgetting her nursling (22:2) and the flight from a brother (80:34–37). Qatāda, Mujāhid and later sources emphasize personal preoccupation; Ibn Kathīr says this holds despite seeing kin in the worst state and cites Ibn ʿAbbās via al-ʿAwfī: they recognize then flee. Al-Ālūsī prefers Qatāda's first report as the most terrifying explanation. Elmalılı says they cannot even ask about a nearby person, still less search for someone farther away. Bursevī argues that if kin do not speak, strangers certainly will not. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ takes this as evidence of the Day's severity."}, {"id": "70:10/q04/p2", "position": "No inquiry is needed because each person's condition is visible or recognizable.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says it is known from features. Qatāda says everyone can see the other's condition; al-Ṭabrisī's anonymous explanation specifies black faces and blue eyes of disbelievers versus radiant color and white faces of believers. Al-Ṭabrisī also invokes 'they see them' in 70:11. Al-Ālūsī gives Qatāda's second report that the state is plain. Al-Biqāʿī says sight rules out concealment as the reason for no question, while he favors distraction."}, {"id": "70:10/q04/p3", "position": "One close person does not ask another for help or benefit, knowing none can be given.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān state this for the active reading. Al-Ālūsī quotes al-Baḥr for it but prefers Qatāda's first, more alarming explanation. Al-Biqāʿī adds that no soul can help another and kinship ties dissolve; only piety matters."}, {"id": "70:10/q04/p4", "position": "One close person does not ask another to bear his sins, having despaired of such help.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan is named by al-Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī. Abū Ḥayyān also records this explanation; al-Ālūsī gives the despair motive. On the passive reading, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī phrase it as no one being asked to take a relative's sins upon himself."}, {"id": "70:10/q04/p5", "position": "No one asks a close person to intercede for him.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān includes intercession among the explanations; al-Ālūsī reports it as a separate view. Al-Ṭabrisī juxtaposes the plea in 26:101 that there is no intercessor or close friend."}, {"id": "70:10/q04/p6", "position": "On the passive reading, no one asks, summons, or calls for a close person to appear or provide aid.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says everyone, criminal and believer, bears an identifying mark, so no one has to be summoned. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī list being summoned or asked to come; al-Ālūsī also mentions help."}, {"id": "70:10/q04/p7", "position": "On the passive reading, no relative is questioned or held accountable for another's deeds or sins.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī cites 74:38, each soul being responsible for its own deeds. Al-Nasafī adds that no one is accountable for another's sin. Al-Biqāʿī compares worldly rulers holding a favored person's kin responsible; God's power applies equally to all. Ibn ʿAṭiyya also transmits an explanation that no one is questioned about another's sin and deeds for accountability."}, {"id": "70:10/q04/p8", "position": "On the passive reading, no one asks a relative about where the other relative is or about the other's condition.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ paraphrases the passive as asking a friend where his friend is but rejects it as contrary to the agreed reading and exegesis. Al-Wāḥidī repeats the objection yet says Ibn Kathīr's passive can mean learning the other's condition. Al-Baghawī and Ibn al-Jawzī give the 'where' wording. Al-Ṭabrisī likens it to ordinary friends and relatives asking after one another. Al-Ālūsī gives condition inquiry as another passive explanation. QIRAAT-ER describes the passive as inability to ask."}, {"id": "70:10/q04/p9", "position": "With the second ḥamīm omitted, close associates recognize one another.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj connects this shorter reading to 'they see them' in 70:11; he contrasts the included-word reading, where one relative does not ask about another."}]}
{"id": "70:10/q05", "question": "What does the indefinite repetition of ḥamīm convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "70:10/q05/p1", "position": "It extends the scene to every pair of close people.", "reasons": "Bursevī explicitly says the indefinite wording generalizes the statement to every close-friend pair; al-Ṭabrisī observes that plural language can refer to many intimates despite singular ḥamīm."}]}
{"id": "70:10/q06", "question": "How does the sight of others in the next verse bear on this verse?", "turns_on": "Who is seen in 70:11, and whether sight supplies recognition, makes inquiry unnecessary, or sharpens the terror of failing to ask.", "positions": [{"id": "70:10/q06/p1", "position": "People see or recognize one another, so their failure to ask occurs despite visibility.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says they see and recognize each other. Al-Zajjāj links the shorter reading to recognition. Al-Ṭabrisī says seeing removes the need to ask; al-Baghawī, cited by al-Biqāʿī, says every human or jinn is in view of a companion. Ibn Kathīr reports Ibn ʿAbbās through al-ʿAwfī: recognition is followed by flight. Al-Biqāʿī says absence of questions comes from self-concern, not concealment. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the suffering friend is seen and the omitted object of asking is therefore clear. Asad likewise says friends can see one another."}, {"id": "70:10/q06/p2", "position": "In the reading that retains the second ḥamīm, those seen may be angels.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj proposes this for the retained-word construction while taking the verse itself to say no relative asks about another."}]}
{"id": "70:10/q07", "question": "How does this verse fit the surrounding Day of Judgment scene and related verses?", "turns_on": "The notes trace different parts of the same scene: the earlier cosmic and fire imagery, visible but neglected intimates, later ransom, and parallels elsewhere in the Qurʾān.", "positions": [{"id": "70:10/q07/p1", "position": "It shows terror dissolving ordinary kinship concern, between cosmic upheaval and the criminal's escalating wish to ransom himself with relatives and all humanity.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the opening 'day when the sky...' can be a new sentence, with this statement replacing an embedded subject; terror explains the failure to ask and frames the ransom wish. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ traces the escalation from intimates not asking to ransom with ever dearer relatives and everyone on earth. Iṣlāḥī combines cosmic upheaval, collapse of social bonds, the family and tribal ransom, and Hell seizing those who avoided the call and hoarded wealth. Kur'an Yolu attributes the willingness to sacrifice spouse, children, close kin and all earth to the sinner's psychological terror. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes that the citation proceeds from the sky like muhl in 70:8 to this verse; her accompanying note quotes al-Rāghib on the preceding fire's flame becoming still and al-Qurṭubī that this does not reduce torment."}, {"id": "70:10/q07/p2", "position": "Other Qurʾānic passages depict each person occupied with himself, fleeing family, and unable to carry another's burden.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī cites 22:2 and 80:34–37. Al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī and StudyQuran cite 80:37. Ibn Kathīr also cites 31:33, 35:18, 23:101 and 80:34–37; StudyQuran mentions 23:101, 31:33 and 35:18. Al-Ṭabrisī also sets this beside 26:101, the absence of intercessors and close friends."}]}
{"id": "70:10/q08", "question": "Who is the sinner described in the surrounding scene?", "turns_on": "Whether the surrounding designation is restricted to unbelievers or extends to sinners generally.", "positions": [{"id": "70:10/q08/p1", "position": "The sinner may refer to unbelievers.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu reports this as one explanation of the sinner in the surrounding passage."}, {"id": "70:10/q08/p2", "position": "The sinner may refer more generally to sinners.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu reports this as the broader explanation of the sinner in the surrounding passage."}]}

{"id": "70:13/q02", "question": "Why is this kin group called faṣīla?", "turns_on": "The notes give either branching from a lineage or a separated bodily piece as the image, and al-Ālūsī disputes which side is described as separating.", "positions": [{"id": "70:13/q02/p1", "position": "The name evokes separation from the kin or ancestral stock from which a person descends.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī derives it from cutting and a subgroup separated from the tribe by an ancestor. {"id": "70:13/q05", "question": "How is تُـْٔوِيهِ read or eased?", "turns_on": "The easing of the hamza, whether its substitute is assimilated, and the vowel or replacement of the final pronoun; authorities cite transmission, the rasm, analogy, and ease of speech.", "positions": [{"id": "70:13/q05/p1", "position": "Its hamza is replaced with a matching glide, without assimilation.", "reasons": "Al-Kāfī and al-Tabṣira prefer this for tuʾwīhi and ruʾyan; al-Tabṣira calls it established practice. Al-Taysīr presents this and assimilation equally, followed by al-Shāṭibī. The Qirāʾāt note describes Ḥamza's easing as loss of the glottal stop and lengthening, without a change in meaning. Ibn al-Jazarī favors clear articulation over assimilation in the comparison with ruʾyā as more analogical and the practice of most reciters; he says deletion solely from the rasm is impermissible. He also says readers agree on replacing ruʾyā's quiescent hamza with wāw after ḍamma."}, {"id": "70:13/q05/p2", "position": "Its hamza is replaced and the resulting glide assimilated.", "reasons": "Al-Tadhkira and al-Dānī favor this treatment for tuʾwīhi and ruʾyan, citing explicit transmission from Ḥamza and agreement with the rasm; al-ʿUnwān gives only this form. Al-Taysīr gives it equal standing with replacement alone, followed by al-Shāṭibī. As a comparison, al-Hudhalī, al-Dānī, and others allow Abū Jaʿfar's assimilation of wāw into the following yāʾ in ruʾyā; Ibn Shurayḥ transmits that but considers it weak. Ibn al-Jazarī favors clear articulation there despite assimilation's agreement with the rasm."}, {"id": "70:13/q05/p3", "position": "It is read without hamza.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī reports this reading from Yazīd. The Qirāʾāt note also describes Ḥamza's easing as removing the glottal stop and lengthening the vowel, without changing the meaning; the two accounts differ in their level of phonetic detail."}, {"id": "70:13/q05/p4", "position": "The pronoun hāʾ has its original ḍamma.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Samīn report al-Zuhrī's nominative or ḍamma hāʾ in both tuʾwīhi and tunjīhi; al-Samīn calls it the original vowel."}, {"id": "70:13/q05/p5", "position": "Al-Sūsī leaves the hāʾ unreplaced.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports that replacing it would make the form heavier, whereas substitution is intended to ease pronunciation."}]}
{"id": "70:13/q06", "question": "What does the criminal wish to do with his sheltering kin?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "70:13/q06/p1", "position": "He would offer even his sheltering kin, with his other loved ones and all earth's people, as ransom for himself, but it would not save him.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī defines iftidāʾ as escaping harm by giving something in one's place. {"id": "70:15/q01", "question": "What does kallā mean here, and how does it divide the speech?", "turns_on": "Whether kallā denies the ransom hope or affirms the following statement, and where the pause falls.", "positions": [{"id": "70:15/q01/p1", "position": "It rebukes the criminal's hope of ransom: no ransom will save him, and the Fire is then announced.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj calls it a rebuke and warning that none return. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the new report about a layer of Hell magnifies its horror; al-Baghawī likewise starts a new statement. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the wish may be unspoken or voiced, cites 78:40 and 4:42, and calls the next sentence an explanatory resumption. Al-Bursawī adds that sin has darkened the criminal's condition; the authorities and the Sajāwandī stop sign favor a full pause at kallā. Al-Jishumī reports a derivation from kadhā lā, shortened and doubled for emphasis. Al-Qurṭubī also permits the denial, with the preceding sentence closing at yunjīhi. Al-Iṣlāḥī sets the wish against collapsing family and tribal bonds."}, {"id": "70:15/q01/p2", "position": "It means 'indeed' or 'truly,' introducing an affirmation about the Fire.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports 'indeed' as an alternative. Al-Qurṭubī permits this sense; al-Bursawī's report of him places the close at yunjīhi and begins the next sentence with kallā. Study Quran reports the rendering 'Truly it is a churning fire.' {"id": "70:15/q02", "question": "What does the pronoun in innahā refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether the antecedent is an implied Fire, the visible sight of it, an implicit matter, or an indefinite item explained afterward; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn dispute what can explain the indefinite pronoun.", "positions": [{"id": "70:15/q02/p1", "position": "It refers to Hell or the Fire, understood from the preceding punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, al-Samīn, al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī infer the Fire from the prior mention of punishment; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī likewise identify the Fire or Hell. {"id": "70:17/q12", "question": "What inward meaning is drawn from the Fire calling those who turn away?", "turns_on": "Whether the inward image stresses the lower world's attraction or the soul's failure to orient toward God and the afterlife.", "positions": [{"id": "70:17/q12/p1", "position": "Worldly life and the lower nature act as a fire that draws kindred hearts toward greed and darkness.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī calls worldly life a hell that hooks hearts through greed, accumulation and preference for wealth over family, with few escaping. {"id": "72:1/q01", "question": "Whom is the Prophet told to address with this report?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q01/p1", "position": "Muhammad is to tell his people, especially Quraysh, what God disclosed about the jinn.", "reasons": "Tabrisi says the news was previously unknown to them; Razi and Biqai say it discloses the jinn episode to the Prophet's companions and people; Islahi says Quraysh is the immediate audience."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q02", "question": "What does revelation mean here and how did the Prophet learn of the listening?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q02/p1", "position": "God informed Muhammad by revelation, through Gabriel; he had not learned the jinn's impressions directly.", "reasons": "Wahidi and Qurtubi identify God as revealer; Tabrisi and Biqai mention the angel Gabriel and the passive's magnification; Ibn Ashur argues the wording implies prior ignorance; Islahi says the jinn did not tell him directly. {"id": "72:1/q03", "question": "How is أُوحِىَ read and derived?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb uses the common quadriliteral or a triliteral dialect, and how far initial wāw-to-hamza analogy extends.", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q03/p1", "position": "The common passive reading is ūḥiya, from the four-letter verb awḥā.", "reasons": "Farra says readers unanimously use the passive; Ibn Atiyya calls it the majority reading; Razi reports an alif in awha; Abu Hayyan and Samin call it the quadriliteral form."}, {"id": "72:1/q03/p2", "position": "A rare reading uses the synonymous triliteral waḥiya or waḥā, retaining initial wāw.", "reasons": "Nahhas, Ibn Atiyya, Tabrisi, Abu Hayyan, Samin and Alusi cite al-Ajjaj's line waḥā lahā al-qarār as evidence. {"id": "72:1/q04", "question": "Why is the revealer left unnamed in أُوحِىَ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q04/p1", "position": "The passive magnifies and gives prominence to God's revelation.", "reasons": "Jishumi calls the unnamed agent a mark of glorification; Tabrisi says God sent it through an angel; Biqai says the passive foregrounds the revelation from the one revealer."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q05", "question": "How does أَنَّهُ ٱسْتَمَعَ function in the passive sentence?", "turns_on": "Whether a prepositional phrase may serve as deputy subject while the revealed content remains accusative.", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q05/p1", "position": "The opened anna clause, meaning the jinn's listening, is the passive subject of ūḥiya.", "reasons": "Akhfash says it is the revelation's content; Nahhas calls it nominative; Zamakhshari, Baydawi, Nasafi, Razi, Samin and Ibn Ashur make the nominalized clause deputy subject. {"id": "72:1/q06", "question": "How are the sūra's following inna and anna clauses read and connected?", "turns_on": "Whether each clause is God's disclosure or the jinn's reported speech, and whether opened clauses attach to ūḥiya or to their affirmation.", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q06/p1", "position": "The opening annahu is fatḥa and the quoted innā samiʿnā is kasra; subsequent revelation clauses open and jinn speech clauses break.", "reasons": "Farra and Zajjaj report agreement on innā here; Nahhas, Kashshaf, Razi, Nasafi, Bursevi, Elmalili and Biqai explain kasra as independent speech after qālū. Ibn Atiyya rejects a purported Abu Amr kasra at 72:1 as unestablished; Tabrisi warns Abu Jafar transmission and its rule disagree."}, {"id": "72:1/q06/p4", "position": "Later innā clauses are generally kasra, with only the opening annahu excepted.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba calls the alternation and speaker attribution a difficulty of the sūra and states this overall pattern; Farra reports Asim's extensive kasra. His description of case as genitive is preserved as reported."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q07", "question": "Where does recitation stop in the later linked clauses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q07/p1", "position": "With kasra at 72:19 stop at 72:18; with fatḥa carry the syntactic connection through 72:19.", "reasons": "Burhan and the Mustawfa author in Itqan connect the stop to the variant reading; Burhan says dependent quoted speech cannot be severed from its governing phrase and rejects an oath analysis at 72:16. {"id": "72:1/q08", "question": "May the transferred vowel in قُلْ أُوحِىَ receive rawm or ishmām at pause?", "turns_on": "Whether a temporary transferred vowel behaves like an intrinsic inflectional vowel at pause.", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q08/p1", "position": "No: its ḍamma is transferred and disappears at pause, so it cannot license rawm or ishmām.", "reasons": "Nashr distinguishes intrinsic from transferred vowels, excludes quiescent forms and non-nunated fatḥa, permits sukun or rawm with intrinsic or connected kasra but not ishmām, and rejects Makki's plural-mim analogy because mim lacks a prior vowel."}, {"id": "72:1/q08/p2", "position": "Makki permits rawm and ishmām for connected plural mīm by analogy with pronoun hāʾ.", "reasons": "Nashr reports and rejects this analogy: plural mim has no prior vowel."}]}
